segments.narration: A physicist watched one funnel for fifty-two years and saw nothing. John Mainstone took charge of the pitch drop experiment in 1961.
Thomas Parnell poured hot pitch into a sealed funnel at the University of Queensland in 1927. He cut the stem three years later.
Then it just hung there. Pitch looks like a solid you could shatter, but it flows, over a hundred billion times thicker than water.
Nine drops have fallen in ninety-nine years. Mainstone missed the 1988 one by stepping out for a drink, and a webcam failed in 2000.
He died in 2013, months before the ninth drop broke free. Nobody has ever seen one fall in person.

verdicts.claim: John Mainstone supervised the University of Queensland pitch drop experiment from 1961 until his death in 2013 and never saw a drop fall.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives Mainstone as supervisor from 1961 to 2013; the University of Queensland page states that neither Parnell nor Mainstone lived to see a drop fall.

verdicts.claim: Thomas Parnell poured hot pitch into a sealed glass funnel at the University of Queensland in 1927 and the funnel stem was cut in 1930.

verdicts.claim: The pitch in the experiment has been estimated at over a hundred billion times the viscosity of water.
verdicts.note: 100% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: Nine drops have fallen since the experiment began; Mainstone missed the seventh drop in July 1988 after stepping out for a drink, and a webcam failed to capture the eighth drop in 2000.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia dates the seventh drop to about 4:45 p.m. on 3 July 1988 and says apparently no one witnessed it because Mainstone had stepped out for a drink; the eighth fell on 28 November 2000. Both sources give nine drops fallen, with a tenth forming.

verdicts.claim: Mainstone died on 13 August 2013 and the ninth drop separated from the funnel on 24 April 2014.
verdicts.note: 88% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 4 number(s)
